title: Ancient Trees in Taiwan: Places to Explore
meta_description: Taiwan's oldest trees are mountain conifers like the Bilu Sacred Tree, over 3,000 years old. Taipei adds camphors, pines, and a ginkgo.
intro:
Taiwan's oldest trees are almost all conifers found deep in mountain forest rather than in a city park, on slopes too steep for the logging that cleared most of the island's lowland giants. The Bilu Sacred Tree, a Taiwan fir put at over 3,000 years, and the Sianglin Sacred Tree, a red cypress whose age is disputed between a newly measured 626 years and a long-quoted 2,300, both stand alone in remote reserve forest rather than beside any town.

Chishang's contribution is deliberately different: a fifty-year-old Bishop wood known not for its age but for a shampoo advertisement filmed beneath it in 2001, which turned an ordinary field tree into one of the island's most visited photo stops. Taipei holds the rest of what is mapped so far: a three-hundred-year-old camphor at Zhishan Rock, a stand of Ryukyu pines known as the Common Three Pines, junipers planted at the Confucius Temple in 1962, and a ginkgo on a university campus. Between them they cover most of what an ancient tree can be here, from a shrine-grove giant nobody has fully aged to a tree made famous by something that happened to it decades after it was already grown.
